subtitle: People say, he claims, and reporting in the Konjunktiv I
words.intro: At a German kiosk there is a tabloid with a headline you can read from across the road. Next to it there’s a serious paper with a headline you can’t. Both, in their own way, keep their distance from what they tell you.

grammar[0].subheading: Who makes the claim? Now, then and passive
grammar[0].blocks[0].title: Who makes the claim?
grammar[0].blocks[1].title: Now, then, passive
grammar[0].blocks[2].title: Rumour or demand?
grammar[0].blocks[2].text: *Der Minister soll zurücktreten* usually means someone demands it. For the rumour: *soll zurückgetreten sein* or *soll zurücktreten wollen*.
grammar[0].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[0].fact: German newsrooms have a rule of thumb for a claim: name the source, or use *soll*. And *will* is sharper than it looks: *Er will nichts gewusst haben* tells the reader that the writer doesn’t believe him, without printing a word that could be sued.

grammar[1].subheading: Is the Konjunktiv I clear? Everything in one past, and not in a formal text
grammar[1].blocks[0].title: Is the Konjunktiv I clearly different?
grammar[1].blocks[0].root.q: Does it look like the normal form?
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Everything in one past
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Not in a formal text
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: *er hätte, es wäre* where *er habe, es sei* exist — speech does it, a report shouldn’t.
grammar[1].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[1].fact: German reported speech has its fallback rule: where the Konjunktiv I looks like the indicative (*sie haben*), switch to the Konjunktiv II (*sie hätten*). Nobody thinks about it while speaking. Editors think of little else.

document.intro: A real front page from a morning in 1914. It’s a very calm headline for what it says. Look at how the paper says who is talking: *Die „Nordd. Allg. Ztg.“ schreibt*. No opinions here, only a source.
document.fact: Germany declared war on Russia that same evening. This was the morning edition, and readers had this page beside their coffee. Papers printed several editions a day then, so the next one would already have looked very different.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Report each with the Konjunktiv I.
reading.intro: A cake has vanished from the fête in Hofstraße. On Monday the local paper has it on page one, and the tabloid has it as well. Vroni, who wrote the first, has brought both to Frau Huber. Frau Huber is the *Augenzeugin*, and she is looking forward to this.
reading.photos[0].caption: Ein Kiosk von früher, mit denselben Schlagzeilen.
reading.photos[1].caption: Ein Zeitungsverkäufer, gemalt: Er soll alles zuerst gewusst haben.
reading.fact: German press law requires care when reporting on anyone who has not been convicted: hence *mutmaßlich*, suspected, and names shortened to *Max B*. The Press Council can publicly reprimand a paper, and the paper is expected to print the reprimand.
